Discontented
dis-kon-TENT-ed
adj. (dissatisfied; uneasy in mind; bitter of soul)
From dis- and content, Latin contentus, held within bounds. The Authorized Version uses it once, of the men who gathered to David in the cave Adullam.

Biblical Definition

And every one that was in distress, and every one that was in debt, and every one that was discontented, gathered themselves unto him; and he became a captain over them: and there were with him about four hundred men. David has escaped to the cave Adullam, and the men who come to him are the least promising army in Scripture: the distressed, the indebted, and the bitter of soul. These four hundred became six hundred, and out of them came the mighty men whose names 2 Samuel records one by one — the three who broke through the host of the Philistines to fetch him water from the well of Bethlehem, and the man who slew a lion in a pit in time of snow. Grace makes something of what it gathers. The dictionary takes the cave as a picture of the church, which has never been assembled out of the qualified, since God hath chosen the weak things of the world, and not many wise men after the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble, are called. What the bitter men in the cave needed, and slowly learned under a captain who would not lift his hand against the LORD's anointed, is what Paul says he had to learn as well: I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): uneasy in mind; dissatisfied; unquiet; in Scripture, describing the men who gathered to David at Adullam, bitter of soul.

expand to see more

DISCONTENTED, a. Uneasy in mind; dissatisfied; unquiet.

DISCONTENT, n. Want of content; uneasiness or inquietude of mind; dissatisfaction at any present state of things.

CONTENTMENT, n. Rest or quietness of the mind in the present condition; satisfaction which holds the mind in peace.

MURMUR, v.i. To grumble; to complain; to utter complaints in a low, half articulated voice.

ADULLAM, n. A city of Judah; also, the cave in which David took refuge.

Key Scripture

1Sa 22:2 — "And every one that was in distress, and every one that was in debt, and every one that was discontented, gathered themselves unto him; and he became a captain over them: and there were with him about four hundred men. was in"

1Sa 22:1 — "David therefore departed thence, and escaped to the cave Adullam: and when his brethren and all his father's house heard it, they went down thither to him."

Php 4:11 — "Not that I speak in respect of want: for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content."

Modern Corruption

Discontent is validated as an authentic response to circumstance and left there, when Scripture treats contentment as something learned, rooted in a promise, and taught to bitter men in a cave.

expand to see more

Paul's statement about contentment is remarkable chiefly for the verb. I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content. It is not a temperament he happened to have and not a state he arrived at once; he says elsewhere in the same paragraph that he learned both how to be abased and how to abound, both how to be full and to be hungry. Contentment in the New Testament is an acquired competence, taught by God through circumstances, and the strength for it is named: I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me.

Hebrews gives the ground rather than the technique, and the ground is a promise about a Person, not a change in the circumstances: let your conversation be without covetousness; and be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee. That is the whole argument. The reason a Christian may be content with what he has is that he cannot be left by the One who has him. The men in the cave were in real distress and real debt, and nothing in the text minimises it; what changed them was a captain worth following and a God who kept his word about a throne.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew mar nephesh (H4751, H5315), bitter of soul; matsowq (H4689), distress or straitness; nasha' (H5378), to lend on interest, and so to be in debt.

expand to see more

Hebrew mar (H4751) — bitter; with nephesh, bitter of soul, rendered discontented.

Hebrew nephesh (H5315) — the soul, the self, the life; the seat of the bitterness.

Hebrew matsowq (H4689) — straitness, distress; every one that was in distress.

Hebrew nasha' (H5378) — to lend or exact, and so a debtor; every one that was in debt.

Greek autarkes (G842) — self-sufficient, contented; therewith to be content.

Usage

"“every one that was discontented, gathered themselves unto him” — the single occurrence."

"“I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content” — a learned grace."

"“I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee” — the ground of it."
